translations.heroSideHtml:
IT, business and compliance expertise

OLING designs and manages projects involving ERP, data governance, cybersecurity, GDPR, quality standards (ISO 27001, Qualiopi), business process transformation and business-side IT project management.

Innovation & operational excellence

Our approach combines active monitoring, continuous R&D and innovative tools, including MAPSI, to anticipate regulatory and technological developments and deliver lasting efficiency for our clients.

Performance and budget control

Our services are designed to deliver a rapid return on investment through a modular, tailored and pragmatic approach that fully reflects each organisation’s budget constraints.
translations.bodyHtml:
Our mission

To be a trusted partner for scoping, managing and securing our clients’ IT, regulatory and organisational projects, with practical, well-controlled solutions that comply with the most demanding standards.

Our areas of expertise

IT project advisory, ERP, CRM, CMMS, cybersecurity, GDPR, ISO audits, quality, safety and environment, DORA/NIS2 compliance, data governance, Microsoft 365, hybrid infrastructure, risk management, and business continuity and disaster recovery.

Our approach

A collaborative approach based on listening, close engagement with operational teams, agility and a proven methodology informed by ISO, CNIL, ITIL and DevOps best practices. Our deliverables focus on results and user adoption.

Our commitment to quality

OLING is ISO 27001:2022 certified. Our internal processes are aligned with the strictest quality and security standards to maintain a high level of excellence in every project we deliver.

A certified multidisciplinary team

Certified Data Protection Officers, ISO auditors, IT project advisory managers, systems and cloud engineers, cybersecurity experts and Qualiopi trainers. OLING assigns an agile, qualified team to every engagement.

Join us

Would you like to contribute to IT, compliance and organisational projects that deliver real value to clients? Join OLING, a fast-growing consultancy where you can develop in a stimulating, demanding and supportive environment.

translations.heroIntro: A clear methodology for turning a regulatory obligation into practical risk management.
translations.heroSideHtml:
DPIA: definition and obligations

A DPIA, or Data Protection Impact Assessment, is the tool used to assess risks to individuals before implementing potentially sensitive processing. A DPIA is too often seen as a legal formality. In reality, it is a decision-making tool. When conducted properly, it helps you balance business objectives, technical feasibility and an acceptable level of risk.

The principle is simple: before deploying high-impact processing, you document the context, assess the risks, define mitigation measures and decide whether the residual risk is acceptable. You keep a record of decisions and their rationale. This approach is very similar to quality management or project risk management. That is why a DPIA fits naturally into business-side IT project management.

In public organisations, a DPIA is often required for processing involving large volumes, special categories of data or decisions that have a significant effect on service users. In SMEs and mid-sized companies, the most common cases involve HR programmes, customer relationships, video surveillance, behavioural analysis or the interconnection of several cloud tools.

The obligation is not "punitive". It protects your organisation against design errors that become costly at the end of a project: late reconfiguration, suspension of use, user friction and reputational risks. It also helps professionalise discussions between business teams, the IT department, legal, security and senior management.

Cases requiring a DPIA

The right approach is to consider combinations of criteria. A DPIA is generally required when processing combines several risk factors: systematic evaluation of individuals, automated decisions, monitoring, sensitive data, matching datasets, large-scale processing or a high impact in the event of an incident.

For example, an internal HR scoring project, even without artificial intelligence, may require a DPIA if it relies on detailed individual data and influences career management decisions. Similarly, a citizen portal combining strong authentication, usage histories and personal circumstances data may require a DPIA, depending on the extent of the processing.

The best way to avoid omissions is to introduce a screening process very early, during project scoping. A questionnaire of 10 to 15 questions is often enough to guide the decision: DPIA required, recommended or unnecessary. This decision must be recorded in your processing register and project documentation.

A six-step methodology

Step 1 - Define the processing and its purpose

Precisely define the business need, functional scope, stakeholders and affected populations. Avoid overly broad wording. A well-drafted purpose is a safeguard in itself: it limits opportunistic uses and clarifies the expected controls.

Step 2 - Map data and data flows

Identify data categories, their sources, the transformations applied, recipients and potential transfers. This step must include interfaces, exports, logs and often-overlooked batch processing. Without data flow mapping, your risk analysis will remain incomplete.

Step 3 - Assess necessity and proportionality

Ask the central question: are you collecting only what is necessary to achieve the objective? Are less intrusive alternatives available? This is often the most valuable step because it can simplify processing before you invest in technical controls.

Step 4 - Assess risks to individuals

Build a clear matrix covering: scenario, severity, likelihood, initial score, proposed measures and residual score. Consider practical consequences: discrimination, exclusion from a service, loss of confidentiality, identity theft, reputational harm and administrative stress. A DPIA examines risks to individuals, not only to the organisation.

Step 5 - Define and prioritise measures

Combine technical, organisational and contractual measures: data minimisation, pseudonymisation, granular access management, export restrictions, audit logs, periodic reviews, processor clauses and user training. Prioritise them by impact and effort. Each measure must have an owner and a target date.

Step 6 - Approve, decide and monitor

The final decision can take one of three forms: authorised launch, conditional launch or suspension pending additional measures. This decision must be formally approved. Monitoring should then be integrated into the project committee: the DPIA does not end when the document is signed; it continues throughout implementation and operation.

Expected deliverables and audit evidence

A robust DPIA file contains: a scoping document, data flow map, necessity and proportionality assessment, risk matrix, treatment plan, formal decision and review records. Auditors are not looking for formal perfection. They look for consistency between identified risks, decisions made and measures actually implemented.

In practical terms, you must be able to demonstrate:

  • The date and context of the assessment.
  • The stakeholders involved.
  • The assumptions used.
  • The trade-offs made.
  • Outstanding actions and how they are managed.

This ability to provide evidence is an operational advantage. It makes discussions with enterprise customers, authorities, cyber insurers and institutional partners more efficient. It also strengthens internal maturity because teams better understand why certain rules exist.

How to integrate a DPIA into business-side IT project management

The most common mistake is starting the DPIA too late, once technical choices have already been finalised. In that situation, the assessment becomes defensive and generates rework costs. Best practice is to integrate it into the IT project lifecycle from the scoping phase onwards.

During the pre-project phase, the screening questionnaire determines whether a DPIA is needed. During the design phase, data protection requirements are integrated into the backlog and acceptance criteria. During acceptance testing, the controls resulting from the DPIA are verified. During the operational phase, quarterly monitoring checks for deviations.

This approach creates a shared language between business teams, the IT department and compliance. It reduces last-minute conflicts and helps keep schedules on track. It is particularly effective for ERP, HR, public service relationship, data platform and portal modernisation programmes.

Post-DPIA action plan template

An effective post-DPIA plan should fit on one actionable page. For each action, it must include: objective, owner, deadline, dependencies, completion indicator and expected evidence. Avoid abstract wording such as "strengthen security". Use measurable actions instead: "enable MFA for all administrator profiles by 30 June", "remove unlogged exports", or "implement an access log for table X".

Recommended structure:

  • Quick wins, 0-30 days: simple corrections with high impact.
  • Stabilisation, 30-90 days: foundational controls and documentation.
  • Industrialisation, 90-180 days: automation, monitoring and training.

Add a short monthly review and a high-level quarterly review. This schedule maintains momentum and prevents the DPIA from becoming a paper exercise.

Practical example: restarting an HR project through a DPIA

A multi-site organisation had launched a cloud-based HR tool to centralise appraisals, mobility and training plans. The project was stalled because several stakeholders were concerned about excessive use of individual data. The team restarted it through a structured DPIA involving workshops with business teams, the IT department, HR, employee representatives and the Data Protection Officer.

Results included: clarified purposes, removal of unnecessary fields, segmentation of access rights, an adjusted retention policy and logging of access to sensitive information. The project resumed with a controlled schedule and stronger internal acceptance.

This case illustrates a key point: a well-timed DPIA does not slow down a project; above all, it prevents late-stage obstacles and poorly documented disputes.

Quick FAQ

Are DPIAs only for large organisations?

No. SMEs and mid-sized companies may also be affected whenever processing presents a high risk to individuals.

Must the DPIA be redone after every change?

Not in full. Conduct an impact review after each significant change and update the relevant sections.

Who signs off the final decision?

Senior management or the controller, informed by assessments from business teams, the IT department, security and the Data Protection Officer.

translations.heroTitle: Choosing an IT project advisory consultancy for SMEs and mid-sized companies: the decisive scorecard
translations.heroIntro: A selection methodology designed to safeguard your budgets, timelines and results.
translations.heroSideHtml:
The 7 selection criteria that truly make a difference

Choosing an IT project advisory consultancy for an SME or mid-sized company is a strategic decision. The right choice accelerates your projects, reduces risk and increases ROI. The wrong choice has the opposite effect: dependency, delays, deliverables that are difficult to act on and internal fatigue. A practical selection scorecard helps prevent these issues.

Criterion 1 - Ability to align business and IT

The consultancy must be equally fluent in business operations and information systems. If it does not understand your business challenges, it will produce impractical technical recommendations. If it lacks command of IT, it will underestimate implementation constraints.

Criterion 2 - A clearly defined delivery methodology

Ask for a clear methodology covering phases, deliverables, milestones, roles and risk management. A promise of a "tailored" approach without a delivery framework is often a warning sign.

Criterion 3 - Ability to provide evidence

The consultancy should present references comparable to your context: organisation size, project complexity and regulatory constraints. Evidence should be factual, including results achieved, deadlines met and risks reduced.

Criterion 4 - A knowledge-transfer culture

A good partner does not create dependency. It transfers best practices, equips your teams and leaves you with sustainable internal capabilities.

Criterion 5 - Integrity when defining scope

The consultancy must know when to say no. Be cautious if it promises everything immediately. The ability to challenge the scope is often a sign of maturity.

Criterion 6 - Command of quality, cybersecurity and GDPR requirements

Modern IT transformation cannot ignore these areas. The consultancy must be able to integrate them from the scoping stage rather than treating them as an afterthought.

Criterion 7 - Robust engagement governance

You need to understand how the engagement will be managed: who will be involved, how often, what reporting will be provided and how issues will be escalated.

Questions to ask before signing

The quality of your questions determines the quality of your decision. Here is a useful set:

  • How do you turn a business requirement into an executable roadmap?
  • What deliverables do you provide within the first 6 weeks?
  • How do you prioritise when the scope exceeds the budget?
  • How do you manage supplier dependency risks?
  • What is your approach to change management?
  • How do you integrate cybersecurity and GDPR into project scoping?
  • Which KPIs do you use to measure the value delivered?

Ask for practical examples rather than generic principles. A strong consultancy can illustrate its methodology with real cases.

Warning signs to identify

Some warning signs should put you on alert during the selection phase:

  • Very long proposals without a clear implementation plan.
  • No named individuals accountable for the engagement.
  • Refusal to define measurable interim deliverables.
  • Discussions focused too heavily on tools and not enough on business objectives.
  • Limited transparency about assumptions and constraints.
  • No skills-transfer plan.

Another important warning sign is confusion between business-side IT project advisory and technical integration. These two areas can coexist, but they must remain distinct to avoid conflicts of interest.

Contractual scoping model and deliverables

A well-defined contract protects both parties. It should include:

  • Engagement objectives and success criteria.
  • In-scope and out-of-scope items and assumptions.
  • Deliverables with a clear definition of "done".
  • Governance, management cadence and decision-making process.
  • Procedures for managing scope changes.
  • A minimum RACI framework covering the client and consultancy.
  • Skills-transfer arrangements.

In terms of deliverables, an initial engagement package may include:

  • Initial assessment covering business, IT and risks.
  • Prioritised scoping document.
  • Phased roadmap.
  • Delivery management plan and dashboard.
  • Change management plan.

This foundation makes the engagement manageable and reduces misunderstandings.

How to measure the ROI of an IT project advisory engagement

The ROI of an IT project advisory engagement can be measured through tangible outcomes:

  • Shorter lead times for critical decisions.
  • Less rework and fewer late-stage changes.
  • Better control of budget, timelines and scope.
  • Fewer post-deployment incidents.
  • Improved user adoption.
  • Reduced risk of non-compliance.

ROI measurement must begin at the outset. Define a baseline when the engagement starts, then track quarterly indicators. Without a baseline, it is impossible to distinguish perception from reality.

Do not overlook intangible benefits, which are often substantial: better collaboration across teams, clearer decision-making, reduced project tensions and greater confidence among senior management.

Example decision scorecard

To compare several consultancies, you can use a 100-point scorecard:

  • Business and IT understanding: 20
  • Methodology and deliverables: 20
  • Comparable references: 15
  • Governance and proposed team: 15
  • Integration of quality, cybersecurity and GDPR: 10
  • Skills transfer: 10
  • Total cost and contractual flexibility: 10

Assign a score to each criterion based on observable evidence. This methodology makes the decision objective and defensible before a committee.

Practical example: an SME choosing a partner

A growing SME needed to launch an ERP project combined with process redesign. Three consultancies were interviewed. The least expensive consultancy proposed a heavily tool-focused approach without a proper change management framework. The most "prestigious" consultancy proposed a senior team with limited availability and a poorly detailed delivery model. The third proposed a phased IT project advisory methodology, clear deliverables, a knowledge-transfer plan and streamlined governance.

The SME chose the third consultancy, with a milestone-based contract and measurable success criteria. Within six months, the project remained within a controlled scope, decisions were made smoothly and the internal teams became more autonomous.

Quick FAQ

Should you choose the best-known consultancy?

Not necessarily. The relevance of its methodology and its fit with your context matter more than brand recognition.

Is the lowest price a good sign?

Not on its own. Consider the total cost, delivery capability and rework risks.

Can you require a skills-transfer plan?

Yes. It is strongly recommended to reduce dependency and strengthen your autonomy.

Learn more

To define your requirements, start with IT project advisory, then tailor your approach with Public sector, SMEs and mid-sized companies. If your priorities include governance and performance, see Quality consulting. To scope your engagement, contact us via Contact OLING.

A 3-phase engagement model to reduce selection risk

A highly effective way to reduce contractual risk is to structure the collaboration in three progressive phases.

Phase 1 - Short targeted assessment (4 to 6 weeks)

Objective: assess the consultancy's actual quality of work in your specific context. Expected deliverables: prioritised assessment, target vision and initial decisions. This phase should already demonstrate the partner's ability to bring business teams, IT and senior management together.

Phase 2 - Detailed scoping and roadmap

Objective: turn the assessment into an executable roadmap. Expected deliverables: prioritised backlog, governance, risks, schedule, budget and change plan. This is where you validate the methodological robustness and quality of interactions.

Phase 3 - Managed implementation support

Objective: test the value delivered through an initial, practical work package with indicators. Expected deliverables: project management, decisions, evidence of results and skills transfer. This phase confirms whether the consultancy can deliver sustainably over time.

This phased model allows you to make decisions based on progressive evidence rather than initial promises.

How to organise an IT project advisory tender without losing focus

An effective IT project advisory tender should be precise enough to support comparison while remaining open enough to allow relevant approaches to emerge. A few high-impact rules:

  • Describe your business challenges before specifying tool requirements.
  • Require interim deliverables and acceptance criteria.
  • Request a complete governance proposal covering forums, cadence and roles.
  • Require a skills-transfer plan.
  • Assess the quality of the actual team, not just showcase CVs.
  • Include a presentation based on a practical case and decision-making scenarios.

The evaluation should combine document analysis with a practical exercise. A 90-minute presentation based on a real-world case will quickly reveal a consultancy's delivery capabilities.

Contract clauses that protect value

Certain clauses are essential to safeguarding your investment:

  • A quarterly review clause covering objectives and scope.
  • A clause governing the replacement of key personnel under specified conditions.
  • A transparency clause covering assumptions and dependencies.
  • A documentation and methodology transfer clause.
  • A controlled exit clause ensuring business continuity.

These clauses are not intended to make the relationship more restrictive. They create a healthier collaboration by making the operating rules explicit from the outset.

translations.heroTitle: Cybersecurity roadmap for SMEs and mid-sized companies: a practical 12-month template
translations.heroIntro: A pragmatic plan to reduce risk without slowing down business execution.
translations.heroSideHtml:
Quickly assess cybersecurity maturity

An effective cybersecurity roadmap starts with a clear-eyed assessment of existing maturity. Many SMEs and mid-sized companies skip this step and launch scattered initiatives: an EDR tool here, a password policy there, and an occasional awareness campaign elsewhere. The outcome is often disappointing because investments fail to address root causes or the most likely risks.

The assessment should remain pragmatic. There is no need to launch a six-month audit. A two- to four-week review can already cover the critical areas: governance, identities and access, workstations, servers and cloud, backups, monitoring, supplier management, crisis management and internal culture. The goal is to produce an actionable snapshot that supports decision-making.

In practical terms, you can score each area on a simple scale from 1 to 5 and provide minimum supporting evidence. For example, "backups tested monthly" is more valuable than a statement of intent. This evidence-based approach avoids subjective debates and gives IT management, senior leadership and business teams a shared baseline.

For mid-sized companies, add an assessment by entity or subsidiary. Internal maturity gaps are often greater than expected. For SMEs, focus on the assets that support revenue, customer relationships and service continuity. This prioritisation is the key to a realistic roadmap.

Define priorities based on risks, impacts and obligations

Once maturity has been assessed, priorities must be set. The best framework combines three perspectives: likelihood of risk, business impact and regulatory or contractual obligations. An initiative may be technically relevant but have a low priority if its business impact is limited. Conversely, a simple weakness may become a priority if it exposes a critical activity or a major customer commitment.

A 3x3 matrix makes prioritisation clearer: incident likelihood, impact severity and regulatory exposure. Each initiative is placed in the matrix and then assigned to one of three levels: immediate, planned or opportunistic. This avoids the "everything is urgent" trap that paralyses teams.

Do not overlook external obligations. Between customer requirements, insurer expectations, internal standards, the GDPR and frameworks such as NIS2 or DORA where applicable, compliance pressure can be significant. The right strategy is to turn these obligations into operational controls rather than decorative documentation. Evidence of an active control is always more valuable than a large but unused set of documents.

Action plan: 0-3 months, 3-6 months and 6-12 months

0-3 months: eliminate avoidable risks

The first phase targets high-impact quick wins. Typical measures include MFA for privileged accounts, a review of inactive accounts, stronger remote access controls, basic separation of administrator privileges, offline backups, restoration testing, an inventory of critical assets and patching of internet-exposed vulnerabilities. These measures quickly reduce the attack surface.

Add an awareness campaign focused on real-world scenarios: phishing, CEO fraud, data breaches and cloud-sharing errors. The goal is not to provide training for its own sake, but to change the few risky behaviours responsible for most incidents.

3-6 months: establish the foundations

The second phase strengthens governance and processes. Set up a short monthly cybersecurity committee, formalise roles, document the information security policy, standardise requirements for critical suppliers, introduce a vulnerability management process and establish a measurable patch management cycle.

For monitoring, start with a simple foundation: centralisation of essential logs, alerts for critical events, priority detection scenarios and an incident response procedure. There is no need to aim for a perfect SOC from the outset. Focus on faster detection and a coordinated response.

6-12 months: scale and manage

The third phase builds long-term resilience. Automate repetitive controls, integrate cybersecurity into business-led IT projects, add crisis exercises, professionalise the disaster recovery plan and measure performance through KPIs. This is also the phase in which cybersecurity becomes more closely aligned with quality, business continuity and operational performance.

At this stage, the roadmap should no longer be a static document. It becomes a managed portfolio of initiatives, with quarterly trade-offs and priority reviews based on threats and the business context.

Budget, resources and trade-offs

Budget is always an important consideration. The key is to assess the cost of avoided risk and the cost of poor quality. A service outage, data breach or loss of customer trust often costs far more than preventive measures.

For an SME, the right approach is often to retain decision-making internally while selectively outsourcing execution. You maintain control over priorities and entrust specific technical initiatives to partners as required. For a mid-sized company, the model is more balanced: a structured internal team, occasional external expertise and cross-functional governance.

Trade-offs must be explicit. When an initiative is postponed, document the accepted risk, the reason and the reassessment date. This discipline prevents grey areas and creates a more professional relationship with senior leadership.

Cybersecurity KPIs for committee oversight

An effective cybersecurity committee relies on a small number of meaningful indicators. Examples include:

  • MFA coverage for sensitive accounts.
  • Average remediation time for critical vulnerabilities.
  • Successful restoration rate for tested backups.
  • Number of incidents detected within 24 hours.
  • Percentage of critical suppliers assessed.
  • Roadmap action completion rate.

Add a measure of residual exposure for each area. The goal is not to achieve zero risk, which is impossible in practice, but to demonstrate a tangible and continuous reduction.

Regular review is essential. A KPI consulted once per quarter does not support effective management. A concise monthly dashboard with commentary and links to decisions is far more effective.

Example of information security governance for SMEs and mid-sized companies

A simple and effective model:

  • Executive sponsor: makes trade-offs, champions priorities and approves accepted risks.
  • IT or information security lead: manages the roadmap and coordinates execution.
  • Business representatives: raise constraints and validate operational impacts.
  • Data Protection Officer, quality or legal teams, depending on the context: ensure compliance consistency.
  • External partners: provide technical execution and specialist expertise.

Recommended schedule:

  • Weekly operational meeting (30 min): incidents, blockers and priorities.
  • Monthly governance meeting (60 min): KPIs, budget and schedule trade-offs, and decisions.
  • Quarterly executive meeting (45 min): overall trajectory, residual risks and investments.

This governance model is intentionally lightweight. It fits into busy schedules and produces actionable decisions.

Practical example: a fast-growing multi-site mid-sized company

A mid-sized services company had inconsistent cybersecurity practices across six sites. It had experienced no recent major incidents, but several warning signs were present: successful phishing attacks, overly broad administrator privileges and infrequent restoration tests. Over 12 months, the company implemented a roadmap in three waves.

0-3 months: administrator MFA, critical asset inventory, dormant account review and an initial restoration test. 3-6 months: cybersecurity committee, information security policy, vulnerability management process and critical supplier onboarding. 6-12 months: crisis exercises, centralised logging and quarterly executive dashboards.

Results: fewer high-impact incidents, shorter remediation times and greater customer confidence during pre-contract security reviews. The main success factor was disciplined management, not the multiplication of tools.

Quick FAQ

Should you start by purchasing tools?

Not initially. Start with risk prioritisation and governance. Tools come afterwards to support a clear plan.

Can an SME have a robust cybersecurity roadmap?

Yes. The quality of management matters more than the size of the company.

What is the first indicator to monitor?

The completion rate for priority actions, combined with a residual risk level.

translations.heroTitle: NIS2 and DORA: a pragmatic implementation plan for your teams
translations.heroIntro: How to get started quickly and avoid compliance projects that exist only on paper.
translations.heroSideHtml:
NIS2 vs DORA: what changes in practice

NIS2 and DORA are often mentioned together, sometimes confused, and almost always perceived as a regulatory mountain. The right starting point is to distinguish their respective approaches. NIS2 strengthens cyber resilience requirements for entities considered essential or important across many sectors. DORA focuses more specifically on digital operational resilience in the financial sector and its ecosystem.

In both cases, the message is the same: having written policies is no longer enough. Organisations must demonstrate operational capabilities: active governance, risk management, detection, response, recovery, third-party management and evidence of control. This marks a shift from declarative compliance to compliance through execution.

For senior management, this means cybersecurity is no longer a purely technical matter. It concerns business continuity, customer relationships, governance accountability and sustainable performance. For IT departments and CISOs, the challenge is to turn obligations into a practical management framework.

Organisational impacts on IT, CISOs and business teams

The main impact of NIS2/DORA is organisational. Roles must be clarified, decision-making channels shortened and responsibilities for producing evidence formalised. An information security policy disconnected from operations is not enough. Organisations need functioning processes: vulnerability management, incident response, continuity testing, third-party assessment and management reporting.

The change is equally significant for business teams. They become active contributors to resilience because cyber incidents primarily create business impacts: service disruption, production delays, unavailable information and loss of customer trust. Business teams must therefore participate in crisis exercises, the prioritisation of critical assets and recovery decisions.

For management, the new responsibility is to make explicit risk decisions. Accepting a risk without an audit trail is no longer defensible. Choices, mitigation plans and follow-up activities must be documented. This discipline is demanding, but it strengthens the organisation's overall robustness.

A 90-day plan to launch compliance

Days 0–30: scoping and visibility

First action: appoint an executive sponsor and an operational lead. Without this pairing, the programme will remain theoretical. Second action: map critical assets and processes. Third action: conduct a rapid assessment of existing controls and major gaps.

At the same time, define a minimum dashboard covering critical risks, significant incidents, overdue actions and the coverage level of essential controls. The objective is not absolute precision, but the ability to manage the programme.

Days 30–60: prioritisation and planning

Build a backlog of prioritised workstreams: governance, detection, incident response, continuity, third parties and awareness. For each workstream, define the owner, objective, milestones and expected evidence. Ensure that every action is linked to a specific risk.

Then establish a monthly committee meeting. Decisions must be recorded: risk accepted, risk treated or risk transferred. This traceability is essential to the framework's credibility.

Days 60–90: execution and evidence

Launch visible, measurable actions: MFA and the hardening of privileged access, recovery tests, reviews of critical third parties, alert scenarios and a tabletop crisis exercise. Document the results, gaps and corrective measures. After 90 days, you should be able to demonstrate that the programme exists in practice, not only in presentation slides.

Policies and controls to prioritise

Organisations often get lost in drafting numerous documents. It is better to start with fewer policies that are genuinely applied. Common priorities include:

  • Cyber risk governance and responsibilities.
  • Identity and access management.
  • Vulnerability and patch management.
  • Incident management and communication.
  • Business continuity, recovery and testing.
  • Critical third-party management.

Each policy must be linked to controls that can be verified in practice. Example: access policy -> quarterly access rights reviews, logging of administrator accounts and a defined timeframe for deleting accounts when people leave. This policy-control-evidence link is the key to defensible compliance.

How to avoid compliance projects that exist only on paper

A paper-based compliance project is easy to recognise: extensive documentation, few indicators, limited testing and weak adoption by business teams. Adopt four principles to avoid this.

First principle: one action = one expected item of evidence. If you do not know what evidence to produce, the action is poorly defined. Second principle: conduct a monthly management review based on a short, consistent dashboard. Third principle: integrate resilience requirements into business-side IT project management so that they are addressed from the design stage. Fourth principle: run regular exercises, because resilience must be tested in real-world situations.

Compliance then becomes a consequence of operational maturity rather than a bureaucratic end in itself.

Management dashboard

A good management dashboard should be no longer than one page. It may contain:

  • Top 10 residual risks with trends.
  • Progress on priority workstreams.
  • Major incidents and lessons learned.
  • Coverage level of critical controls.
  • Status of critical third parties, including assessments and remediation plans.
  • Results of continuity tests and crisis exercises.

Each indicator should prompt a decision. If an indicator never triggers discussion or a management decision, it serves no purpose.

Alignment with GDPR, quality and IT performance

NIS2 and DORA do not operate in isolation. They naturally connect with GDPR, quality management and IT performance. Cyber incidents often affect personal data, SLAs and user satisfaction. Unified governance helps avoid duplicate committees and reporting.

In practice, you can align:

  • The critical asset map with the record of processing activities.
  • Business continuity plans with quality processes.
  • Cybersecurity requirements for suppliers with GDPR contractual clauses.
  • Cybersecurity KPIs with service KPIs such as availability, response times and incidents.

This integration is particularly useful for mid-sized companies, where multiple obligations can overwhelm teams. By harmonising frameworks, you reduce the administrative burden and make decision-making clearer.

Practical example: launching a resilience programme in 4 months

An organisation with a strong dependence on digital systems needed to meet new customer expectations regarding resilience. Its main risk was fragmentation: several initiatives existed, but there was no common governance. The programme began with a 4-week scoping phase, followed by a 90-day plan with a monthly management committee.

Key actions included creating an inventory of critical assets, upgrading privileged access controls, formalising incident management, conducting an initial crisis exercise and reviewing major service providers. Within 4 months, the organisation had established a consistent evidence base and a prioritised 12-month roadmap.

The main lesson: speed comes from clear responsibilities and simple governance routines, not from producing more documents.

Quick FAQ

Should NIS2 and DORA be handled through two separate programmes?

Not necessarily. A common resilience foundation can cover a large proportion of the requirements, with sector-specific adjustments.

What is the first useful deliverable?

A map of critical assets and a backlog of prioritised workstreams with assigned owners and evidence requirements.

Who should lead the programme?

An executive sponsor and an operational lead, working closely with IT management, the CISO, business teams and compliance functions.

One final practical recommendation: start small, but make the work visible. Building evidence creates internal buy-in and facilitates subsequent decisions.

translations.heroTitle: Public sector IT transformation: governance, priorities and delivery
translations.heroIntro: A practical roadmap for modernisation without compromising service continuity.
translations.heroSideHtml:
Public sector-specific constraints

Public sector IT transformation takes place in a unique context: service continuity requirements, multiple stakeholders, budgetary pressure, institutional timelines and stringent regulatory requirements. Projects cannot be managed as they would be in a standard private-sector environment, because their impact on service users and public accountability require stronger governance discipline.

Management teams must balance two objectives that may appear contradictory: modernising rapidly while maintaining impeccable service stability. This tension explains why public-sector IT programmes require structured IT project advisory, with careful prioritisation and evidence-based milestones.

Another distinctive feature is that transformation is rarely purely technical. It involves changes to the organisation, business practices, relationships with service users and coordination across departments. Without change management, even a technically robust solution may fail to deliver the expected value.

Build robust programme governance

Governance is at the heart of success. It must answer three questions: who decides, what they decide on and how often. An effective framework combines:

  • A strategic steering committee (management, major decisions).
  • A programme committee (portfolio monitoring, priorities, risks).
  • Operational project committees (delivery, obstacles, deliverables).

Each body must use a standard reporting format covering progress, budget, risks, required decisions and impact on service users. Without this standard, meetings become informative but rarely lead to decisions.

Public-sector organisations also benefit from establishing a cross-departmental RACI. Unclear areas of responsibility are a frequent cause of delays. Clarifying responsibilities is not bureaucratic; it accelerates delivery.

Prioritise high-value initiatives

Public-sector prioritisation cannot be based solely on technical criteria. It must consider value for service users, impact on staff, continuity risks, regulatory obligations and implementation feasibility.

A simple method is to assess initiatives across four dimensions:

  • Impact on the quality of service provided.
  • Reduction of operational and regulatory risk.
  • Transformation effort (organisation + IT).
  • Time required to achieve observable results.

This scoring method distinguishes between "foundation" initiatives, which should begin quickly; "high-leverage" initiatives, which should be scheduled promptly; and "long-term" initiatives, which require preparation. Prioritisation then becomes defensible and shared.

Integrate GDPR, cybersecurity and quality

In the public sector, compliance and service performance are inseparable. A cyber incident affects service users' trust. Poor data management weakens the institutional relationship. Inadequate process quality reduces delivery capability.

Best practice is to integrate these dimensions from the scoping stage:

  • GDPR requirements linked to target processes.
  • Cybersecurity requirements linked to critical assets.
  • Quality requirements linked to service indicators.

This integrated approach prevents corrective projects from being required at the end of the programme. It also streamlines committees and reporting by establishing unified performance and risk governance.

Large-scale change management

Change management is often underestimated, even though it determines actual adoption. Public-sector programmes must address several groups simultaneously: staff, managers, support functions, external partners and, in some cases, service users.

An effective plan is based on five levers:

  • Impact mapping for each stakeholder group.
  • A clear and continuous communication plan.
  • Targeted training by role and use case.
  • A network of local representatives (ambassadors).
  • Adoption measurement with corrective actions.

The objective is not to "convince" people as a matter of principle, but to reduce friction in use and provide rapid evidence of value. When staff see tangible benefits, adoption naturally accelerates.

Impact indicators for decision-makers

A public-sector programme must demonstrate clear results. Useful indicators are those that connect IT transformation with service delivery:

  • Average processing time for a service user request.
  • First-contact resolution rate.
  • Availability of critical digital services.
  • Staff adoption rate for new tools.
  • Number of major incidents and recovery time.
  • Percentage of corrective actions completed on time.

Add a service user perception indicator whenever possible. Perceived quality is both a political and an operational factor.

Typical 12-month roadmap

0-3 months: scoping and foundations

Assessment, governance, prioritised portfolio, major risks and initial action plan. The objective is to establish a clear roadmap.

3-6 months: initial high-value deployments

Launch of quick-impact initiatives, implementation of KPIs, adjustment of critical processes and strengthening of cybersecurity and GDPR controls.

6-9 months: expansion and harmonisation

Progressive rollout, cross-departmental alignment, stabilisation of practices and enhanced user support.

9-12 months: industrialisation

Automation of controls, overall performance review, consolidation of benefits and preparation for the next cycle.

This roadmap does not claim to eliminate all complexity. Above all, it makes the programme predictable and manageable.

Practical example: multi-site local authority

A large local authority needed to modernise several areas: service user relationships, internal processes, collaboration tools and data management. The main risk was the fragmentation of initiatives. The programme was refocused around unified governance, prioritisation based on value for service users and early integration of GDPR, cybersecurity and quality.

Within nine months, the local authority reduced processing times across several service user journeys, stabilised the availability of critical services and improved cross-departmental coordination. The decisive factor was management discipline: documented decisions, updated risks and concise, action-oriented reporting.

Quick FAQ

Can transformation happen quickly in the public sector?

Yes, provided that priorities are clear and governance is streamlined, without multiplying approval processes.

Should IT and organisational projects be separated?

No. They must progress together to deliver lasting value.

Which risks should be monitored first?

Service continuity, data quality, supplier dependencies and user adoption.

Learn more

Continue with Public sector, SMEs and mid-sized companies, connect your roadmap with IT project advisory, and strengthen sensitive areas through GDPR and Cybersecurity. To scope a programme tailored to your context, contact us via Contact OLING.

Target architecture and systems planning: avoid transformation debt

Public-sector IT transformation often fails when the target architecture remains implicit. Projects move forward in response to urgent needs and create an accumulation of poorly interoperable local solutions. To avoid this debt, organisations must define simple systems planning principles that can be shared and monitored by project committees.

These principles may include reusing shared services, controlling interfaces, standardising identities, governing master data repositories and establishing minimum security-by-design requirements. The objective is not to restrict innovation, but to ensure the overall consistency of the IT estate.

Well-managed IT project advisory translates these principles into practical decision-making rules. For example, every new digital service must specify its dependencies, data model, continuity plan and GDPR impacts. This discipline reduces unintended consequences and facilitates medium-term maintenance.

Funding, delivery capacity and a multi-year roadmap

In the public sector, funding cannot be separated from the roadmap. Transformation cannot depend solely on annual budget opportunities. A multi-year vision with value milestones is required to secure decisions and maintain momentum.

An effective approach is to structure the programme into fundable value blocks: technical foundations, priority service user journeys, staff tools, data governance and cyber resilience. Each block must include a service objective and an impact indicator.

Delivery capacity must also be addressed explicitly: availability of internal teams, workload planning, use of partners and a sustainable rollout pace. An ambitious schedule without genuine capacity creates fatigue and reduces quality. Conversely, a realistic roadmap with incremental deliverables builds confidence and strengthens political support.

Six-action plan for the next 120 days

  • Approve programme governance and the committee schedule.
  • Finalise the prioritisation of initiatives based on value for service users.
  • Launch two measurable quick wins for critical journeys.
  • Integrate GDPR, cybersecurity and quality requirements into every scoping document.
  • Implement a one-page management dashboard.
  • Organise an initial cross-departmental crisis exercise.

These six actions create momentum without placing an excessive burden on the organisation. They establish the foundations for sustainable, manageable transformation.
